evaluation.positioning_hook: A burned-out orbital depot crew discovers their station is being treated as an insurance asset while reality itself compresses around them, forcing one technician to outthink a system that has already priced them in.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: a contained space thriller with a corporate conspiracy and a survival countdown. The audience is clear and genre-friendly, though the concept plays strongest for thriller buyers and sci-fi fans rather than broad four-quadrant viewers.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early with the insurance valuation reveal, the Sim-Gate anomaly, and the station-wide realization that the crew is being classified as inventory. The story engine is easy to explain in one breath: a depot crew discovers the system around them is turning them into expendable assets as the station begins to fail.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Miller, Sarah, Vance, Dr. Aris, and even Riggs each have a distinct operating style, and the script gives them clear behavioral signatures. Miller carries the center, Sarah brings bite, Vance brings nervous intelligence, and Dr. Aris has the sharpest authority; the ensemble is strong enough to hold the movie, though the emotional interior is still carried more by situation than by deep personal revelation.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s corporate-language horror is distinctive: crew valuation matrices, asset classifications, comfort clocks, and protocol-as-violence give the material a sharp identity. The final reveal of the Technician in the preservation room reframes the whole film with a cold, unsettling elegance.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The escalation is strong and cumulative: anomaly, valuation reveal, quarantine, orbital decay, decompression, crash, loop, escape, and final capture. Each major turn changes the rules of the situation, and the last act keeps tightening the vise until the ending lands with real force.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a corporate orbital depot where the crew is literally reclassified as assets, then compressed by the station itself, feels fresh and immediately legible. It has the rare quality of being strange on first glance and obvious in retrospect.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The depot feels lived-in and operational, with maintenance trusses, Sim-Gate systems, telemetry rooms, PPE protocols, and corporate hierarchy all feeding the story. The world is not just backdrop; it generates the plot mechanics, the language, and the social pressure.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: deadpan workplace banter, Black-coded crew chemistry, bureaucratic dread, and body-horror pressure all coexist without losing the thread. The script knows exactly when to be funny, when to be clinical, and when to go cold.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the survival plot, there are strong ideas about labor, belonging, corporate personhood, and the way systems make people disappear while still calling it procedure. The ending suggests a larger architecture behind the depot, which gives the film a deeper aftertaste.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Miller-Sarah-Vance-Dixon-Riggs web has real friction and chemistry, and several scenes are built on status shifts rather than exposition. The ensemble is functional and lively, though the movie still clearly orbits Miller as the central gravity point.

technical.sfx_needs: Practical lighting shifts, pressure/decompression effects, suit work, and simulated environmental anomalies.

rights_flags.detail: The script references an Andy Williams-style lounge track and a 56K modem sound cue, but no specific licensed song title is named.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Premium streaming or theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: festival-to-platform or limited theatrical genre play

cost.note: Contained interiors keep the footprint manageable, but the orbital exterior work, environment-printing effects, and station-destruction finale push it above a microbudget lane.

cast.note: The ensemble is adult and manageable, but the film benefits from strong chemistry across Miller, Sarah, Vance, Dixon, Riggs, Dr. Aris, and Hendrix.

location.note: Most of the story lives in a limited number of depot interiors, with a few exterior EVA and lifepod-platform sequences adding scale.

content.note: The script includes violence, body-horror pressure, corporate cruelty, and strong language, but it stays within a controlled mature-thriller lane.

rights.note: No real people, branded IP, or named songs are central to the story; the references are atmospheric rather than clearance-dependent.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The corporate horror language is the hook.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the film a marketable identity beyond standard space survival: the dread comes from policy, valuation, and procedure, not just monsters or malfunction. Buyers who want elevated genre with a sharp social angle will see a clean lane for premium streaming or festival launch.
strengths.evidence: The crew insurance valuation matrix, the asset classifications, and Riggs calling the crew operational expenses reimbursable under loss.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Miller is a strong anchor role.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead has the kind of contained intensity that can carry a feature and give an actor a full showcase of restraint, authority, and dawning horror. Mid-career dramatic leads and actors looking for a prestige genre turn will respond to a role that plays intelligence under pressure.
strengths.evidence: Miller’s quiet observation of the pencil, his decision to keep working after the insurance reveal, and his final move to force the crash.

strengths.what_it_means: The banter and status play create a cast dynamic that makes the movie feel inhabited, which helps both audience engagement and trailerable moments. Ensemble-friendly buyers and directors who like performance-driven genre will see multiple playable roles, not just a single hero track.
strengths.evidence: Sarah’s sharp exchanges with Miller and Vance, Dixon’s comic defiance, and Dr. Aris’s dry authority.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world is an engine, not a backdrop.
strengths.what_it_means: The depot systems, Sim-Gate, telemetry, PPE protocols, and orbital mechanics all generate story turns, which makes the setting feel expensive on the page without requiring a sprawling cast. Genre buyers looking for a contained but high-concept sci-fi package will understand the production value immediately.
strengths.evidence: The Sim-Gate environment printing, the orbital decay reveal, the decompression breach, and the station compression logic.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending reframes the whole movie.
strengths.what_it_means: The Technician reveal in the preservation room turns the story from a survival thriller into something colder and more unsettling, which gives the film a memorable aftertaste and franchise-adjacent mythology. Buyers who want a final-image sting that lingers will respond to that last-room reveal.
strengths.evidence: The monochrome diner/preservation room, the Technician’s inventory language, and the drawer of preserved crew boxes.

whats_special.headline: PROTOCOL is a contained sci-fi thriller with a nasty commercial edge: a depot crew discovers they’ve been reduced to line items while the station itself starts compressing around them. It has a clean genre engine, a strong ensemble, and a final-reveal button that turns the whole movie into a cold corporate nightmare.

lead_characters.name: MILLER MCCORD
lead_characters.hook: Miller is the quiet center of the film: observant, exhausted, and hard to read until the pressure forces him into action. He carries himself like a man who has learned to survive by staying still, but the script keeps revealing that his stillness is a form of control, not passivity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Mahershala Ali in a role like True Detective’s most internal leads — a contained, watchful performance where silence does as much work as dialogue. Actors who want to play intelligence, restraint, and a late-breaking command of the room will chase this because the role lets them turn inward pressure into decisive action.

lead_characters.name: SARAH BEAUMONT
lead_characters.hook: Sarah is the sharpest social reader in the crew, funny when she wants to be, cutting when she needs to be, and emotionally the least willing to pretend the system is neutral. She has the kind of lived-in skepticism that makes her feel like she’s been surviving this place longer than the place deserves.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve-style material — fast intelligence, emotional bite, and the ability to pivot from banter to moral clarity in a beat. Actors who want a role with wit, steel, and a strong point of view will see a part that gives them both propulsion and attitude.

lead_characters.name: VANCE MATHESON
lead_characters.hook: Vance is the brainy, twitchy systems guy whose urgency makes him feel like he’s always one thought ahead of the room and one breath behind his own nerves. He’s funny, technical, and emotionally exposed in a way that gives the ensemble a volatile, human pulse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Rami Malek in Mr. Robot or The Pacific-type pressure-cooker intelligence — a role where anxiety, precision, and technical fluency become performance texture. Actors who like playing high-functioning panic with comic timing will be drawn to the part because it lets them weaponize intellect.

lead_characters.name: DR. PATRICIA ARIS
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Aris is dry, unsentimental, and quietly formidable, with the kind of authority that comes from competence rather than volume. She reads as the person in the room most likely to leave first, but also the one most capable of seeing the system clearly enough to survive it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the controlled authority of Olivia Colman in The Favourite or Tilda Swinton in prestige genre work — wit, command, and a razor-clean sense of self. Mid-career and veteran actresses looking for a role that plays intelligence, irony, and survival instinct in one package will chase it.

lead_characters.name: RIGGS
lead_characters.hook: Riggs is the tired middle-manager face of the machine: folksy, evasive, and increasingly revealed as the human voice of a system that treats people as liabilities. He’s not a cartoon villain; he’s the kind of man who can say something monstrous in a calm, managerial tone and still think he’s being practical.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in a prestige antagonist role — a character whose ordinariness is the threat and whose authority collapses into something colder as the story advances. Actors who like playing institutional power with a human mask will want this because it lets them be charming, bureaucratic, and terrifying in the same scene.

lead_characters.name: DIXON
lead_characters.hook: Dixon is the crew’s pressure valve: sharp-tongued, skeptical, and funny enough to keep the room alive even when the situation turns lethal. He reads as a man who knows exactly how absurd the system is and refuses to dignify it with reverence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the fast, scene-stealing rhythm of Walton Goggins in Justified or Lakeith Stanfield in a sharp ensemble — comic timing with real menace underneath. Character actors who can turn sarcasm into survival instinct will chase it.

lead_characters.name: HENDRIX
lead_characters.hook: Hendrix is the physically imposing systems specialist whose size becomes part of the joke and part of the tension, because the station itself seems to resist him. He’s dry, technical, and slightly overclocked, with a body that makes every corridor feel smaller and every problem feel more immediate.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a character actor like J. K. Simmons in a pressure-cooker ensemble — authority, humor, and physical presence doing different jobs at once. Tall performers and actors who can play intelligence with comic friction will be drawn to the part because it gives them a memorable silhouette and strong dialogue.

lead_characters.name: HENDERSON
lead_characters.hook: Henderson is the polished, upper-management voice of the machine: calm, entitled, and insulated enough to sound reasonable while saying things that are deeply dehumanizing. He functions as the remote face of corporate logic, all soft-light professionalism and zero accountability.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play polished menace the way Tom Hiddleston or Matthew Macfadyen can in prestige drama — charm as a delivery system for control. Actors who specialize in elegant authority and passive aggression will see a clean, memorable antagonist slot.

lead_characters.name: ROBERT
lead_characters.hook: Robert is the practical crew member who mostly absorbs the chaos and keeps moving, which makes him feel like the sort of person every workplace depends on and never notices. He’s less verbal than the others, but he gives the depot a grounded, working-body presence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor the lived-in realism of a good ensemble player in a survival thriller — the person who makes the world feel operational. Character actors who can do a lot with presence and reaction will be useful here.

lead_characters.name: ENGINEER #2 / JAMES FORREST
lead_characters.hook: Engineer #2 is the first body the film claims, and James Forrest’s identity becomes part of the story’s cold accounting. He’s a functional crew presence whose death turns the insurance language from abstract to horrifyingly literal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor a memorable early-film impact in the tradition of strong genre ensemble casualties — the kind of part that makes the world feel dangerous because the audience remembers the face. It’s a clean fit for a working character actor who can make a brief appearance land hard.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make corporate dread feel physical.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Mid-career genre directors with at least one contained thriller or elevated sci-fi feature, plus first- or second-feature filmmakers coming out of shorts with a strong visual grammar. This material rewards directors who care about pressure, systems, and performance-forward tension more than spectacle for its own sake.
director_appeal.detail: The film gives a director a chance to stage escalating paranoia inside a controlled industrial environment, then pay it off with a final-image reveal that recontextualizes everything. It’s especially attractive to directors who like making design, blocking, and rhythm do the heavy lifting while keeping the camera close to human behavior.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streamer genre lane / festival-friendly sci-fi thriller
buyer_appeal.detail: The contained cast and mostly interior depot setting make it packageable off a strong director and one or two recognizable leads, without needing a tentpole-level effects spend. The corporate-horror angle and clean survival engine fit the current buyer appetite for elevated genre that can travel well on streaming and still play a limited theatrical or festival launch.

considerations.area: The final reveal can be even more legible.
considerations.detail: The Technician preservation-room sequence is striking and memorable; a next pass could make the reveal’s rules slightly clearer earlier so the ending lands with maximum inevitability. The version of the script where the preservation logic is seeded in one or two earlier beats would make the last image feel even more devastating.

considerations.area: Miller’s interior life is mostly carried by behavior.
considerations.detail: The script gives Miller strong presence and authority, and a future pass could consider one or two more personal beats like the photo of the woman in his locker to deepen the emotional charge of his choices. That would give the climax even more personal voltage without changing the plot engine.

considerations.area: The ensemble chemistry is a major asset.
considerations.detail: The banter between Sarah, Dixon, Vance, and Riggs is one of the movie’s best commercial tools, and the version of the script where a few of those exchanges are allowed to recur as motifs could strengthen trailer moments and audience attachment. This is a positioning note more than a rewrite note: the cast dynamic is already doing real work.

considerations.area: The VFX footprint is contained but meaningful.
considerations.detail: The orbital exterior, Sim-Gate distortions, decompression sequence, and station collapse all point to a moderate effects package rather than a microbudget play. That keeps the film in a realistic premium-genre lane, and the contained depot setting protects the spend by limiting the number of distinct builds.

considerations.area: The cast can be packaged efficiently.
considerations.detail: The story lives on five leads and a few strong supporting roles, which means the project can be built around performance rather than a large-name ensemble. That makes it attractive to buyers who like genre films that can be greenlit with one anchor and a strong supporting bench.
